title: ’addēsh — prices, big numbers and bargaining
goal: Ask prices, understand numbers up to a thousand, bargain without giving offense, and know the currencies of the four Levantine countries.
bekal: ask a price with قَدِّيش and understand the answer
count in tens, hundreds and thousands
bargain with the expressions locals actually use

dialogs.title: حَكِي — بِسُوق الْحَمِيدِيِّة
dialogs.intro: The biggest covered market in Damascus. Budi wants to buy a scarf for his mother, and the trader names his first price.

lines.speaker: اَلْبَيَّاع:
lines.id: Welcome! Go ahead, have a look.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Thanks. How much is this scarf?

lines.speaker: اَلْبَيَّاع:
lines.id: This one's fifty thousand. Real wool.

lines.speaker: اَلْبَيَّاع:
lines.id: Honestly, it's the best kind we have.

lines.speaker: اَلْبَيَّاع:
lines.text: أَكِيد. هَيّ بِتْلَاتِين، بَسّ مِش صُوف.
lines.baca: akiid. hayy bitlaatiin, bass mish ṣuuf.
lines.id: Sure. This one's thirty, but it's not wool.
lines.literal: sure. this for-thirty, but not wool.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: بَدِّي هَاد الْأَوَّل. آخِر سِعِر قَدِّيش؟
lines.id: I want the first one. What's your final price?
lines.literal: want-my this the-first. last price how-much?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.baca: khamse w tlaatiin w baakhdo halla’.
lines.id: Thirty-five and I'll take it now.

lines.speaker: اَلْبَيَّاع:
lines.id: Oh, all right, for you. Take it.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Thanks a lot. Here's the money.

lines.speaker: اَلْبَيَّاع:
lines.id: Congratulations! Wear it in good health.

notes: **The word قَدِّيش is the only "how much" you need.** It's used for prices (قَدِّيش هَاد؟), age (قَدِّيش عُمْرَك؟), distance, time and quantity. The Fusha form كَم does exist in the Levant, but it sounds formal.

**Prices are given with the prefix بِـ.** The phrase بِخَمْسِين أَلْف means "for fifty thousand", just like English "for fifty". Saying the number alone without بِـ is still understood and very common.

**Bargaining isn't an insult; it's part of the deal.** In traditional markets the first price is expected to be bargained down, and the trader is actually a little disappointed if you agree straight away. On the other hand, **in modern shops and supermarkets prices are fixed** — bargaining there is out of place.

**The unwritten rule is simple: offer about a third less, then meet in the middle.** The sentence that opens bargaining politely is آخِر سِعِر قَدِّيش؟ ("what's your final price?"). Never bargain for something you don't intend to buy.

**The phrase مِن عْيُونِي literally means "from my eyes".** It means "all right, for you" and is used when someone grants a request. Together with تَكْرَم عَيْنَك from unit 3, it belongs to a family of Levantine expressions that all involve the eyes.
**The word مَبْرُوك is said for any purchase.** For clothes there's a special version: تِلْبْسُو بِالْهَنَا ("may you wear it happily"), answered with يِسْلَمُوا or اَللَّه يْخَلِّيك.

grammars.title: Tens, hundreds, thousands
after: ⚠️ In compound numbers, **the units come first**: خَمْسَة وْتْلَاتِين *khamse w tlaatiin* is literally "five and thirty" for 35 — like the old English "four-and-twenty blackbirds". It takes conscious practice; if in doubt, say the number slowly and let the other person correct you.
Notice that all the tens end in ـِين — one pattern for eight numbers. Once you catch it, the whole series falls into place.

grammars.title: Currencies and how to say prices
after: In everyday conversation **the name of the currency is almost always dropped** when it's clear from context. The answer بِخَمْسِين is enough, and adding لِيرَة actually sounds like reading out a price list.

⚠️ In Lebanon and Syria, strings of zeros are often trimmed in speech: a price of "a hundred thousand" may be said as just مِيِّة. If the number seems too small for the item, ask again with قَدِّيش بِالضَّبْط؟ ("how much exactly?").

blocks.text: The sentence بَدِّي شُوف بَسّ is a lifesaver in any market. It says politely that you're just looking, and Levantine traders will respect it — usually while still offering you a glass of tea.

blocks.title: Saying no without offending
items: The gentlest: اَللَّه يْسَهِّل *alla ysahhil* — literally "may God make it easy". It's a blessing and a refusal at once, and nobody takes offense.
Direct but still polite: مَا بَدِّي، شُكْرًا. Say it with a smile and keep walking.
⚠️ Don't bargain and then walk away once the trader accepts your offer. Across the Levant that's considered bad form — accepting an offer counts as a done deal.

blocks.text: Notice that لَبَن in the Levant means **yogurt**, not milk — a trap for anyone who learned "laban = milk" from Fusha or from Gulf Arabic. Milk is حَلِيب. Mix them up and you'll go home with a liter of yogurt.

blocks.title: Buying by the unit
items: Weight: كِيلُو *kiilu* (kilo) and نُصّ كِيلُو *nuṣṣ kiilu* (half a kilo). The full sentence is كِيلُو تُفَّاح مِن فَضْلَك.
Counting units: حَبِّة *habbe* for fruit and eggs (تْلَات حَبَّات means "three of them"), and رَبْطَة *rabṭa* for a bunch of vegetables.
To ask for more: كَمَان شْوَي *kamaan shway* ("a little more"). To stop: هَيْك بَسّ *hēk bass* or خَلَص.

exercises.prompt: Write the number in Levantine Arabic.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: قَدِّيش هَاد؟ — غَالِي شْوَي. — فِي شِي أَرْخَص؟ — آخِر سِعِر قَدِّيش؟ — بَاخِد هَاد. — بَدِّي شُوف بَسّ.
خَمْسَة وْتْلَاتِين — تْمَانْيِة وْأَرْبَعِين — سَبْعِين — مِيِّة وْخَمْسِين — سِتّ مِيِّة — أَلْفَين وْخَمْس مِيِّة
قَدِّيش — غَالِي — أَرْخَص — تُفَّاح — بَاقِي — خَلَص
قَدِّيش هَاد؟ — هَاد غَالِي كْتِير. — فِي شِي أَرْخَص؟ — هَيّ بِتْلَاتِين أَلْف. — خَمْسَة وْتْلَاتِين وْبَاخْدُو. — بَدِّي شُوف بَسّ.
wave: Say ten random prices out loud — from 21 to 999 — and remember: the units always come first.
